label: Adventure / fantasy RPG: stacked resource bars, enemy nameplates, floating damage numbers, chest inventories, counter-side merchant shops
provenance: Distilled from the eight adventure rows in packages/corpus/data/genre-references.json, each a Roblox Developer Forum topic whose first post and representative images were visually inspected on 2026-09-23 (verification status live_topic_json_verified, referenceUse reference_only, copyPermission false). This file restates those recorded observations as UI construction. It does not re-fetch the pages, and it stores no image, no Luau source and no asset.
honestLimits: Eight forum topics, one to three images each. Four of them are map, lighting or prop studies, so their rows here record what the world asks of the interface (readable routes, lantern chains, landmarks), not a measured HUD.
Nothing was measured with a colour picker or an inspector. No stroke weight, corner radius or bar height is given in px. Proportions are stated as ratios between elements that the observations name.

Two of the UI sources are work-in-progress critiques (the resource-bar study and the chest inventory), and one shop source shows an Explorer hierarchy rather than finished art. They carry structure and hierarchy, not a finished visual target.
No shipped adventure game's live HUD was inspected directly. A quest tracker, minimap or dialogue box is therefore NOT recorded as an adventure convention, and no rule for one is stated here.

demonstrates: three resource bars share ONE frame: a thin experience bar on top, the thickest health bar in the middle carrying a numeric readout, and a thin mana bar below
each resource keeps one colour family, red for health, blue for mana and amber for experience, and a swatch study settles the colours before the art is drawn
the health bar is the focal element, marked by pointed arrow ends and a gold bevelled border, with the number right-aligned inside the fill
an enemy carries a nameplate above its head: name on the left, level on the right, and a segmented red health bar beneath both
damage is a large red number floating above the target, separate from the nameplate, so a hit reads without looking at a bar
the town hub is a central fountain plaza with paths radiating out, so world UI such as nameplates sits over a readable, uncluttered scene
a wide grid of equal square slots sits under a full-width search bar, so the player filters a large chest instead of scrolling it
a footer capacity counter shows the chest name and used-over-maximum slots, keeping the storage limit visible while sorting
dark brown wood tones match the in-world chest, but empty slots sit so close to the panel colour that the grid edges nearly vanish, a visible failure the source itself shows
sale items sit on physical shelves in the world, each with its own price and shelf slot, instead of in a full-screen catalogue
each shelf item has its own buy button and name label on a surface in the world, so browsing happens at the counter where the player already stands
one interact prompt opens the merchant, a camera focus part frames the counter, and the purchase is settled by a server script
at night the road stays navigable because lanterns on posts and distant campfires form a chain of warm points across a dark blue field, so the world, not a HUD arrow, carries the route
a massive rock outcrop with a lantern at its base ends the dirt road as a destination visible over the grass
the packed dirt road stays the palest band of terrain while knee-high grass hides the ground plane
a wooden signpost and a small notice board are the only information surfaces on the path, each placed where the route turns
a dirt path curves from a foreground bridge past the signpost toward village roofs on a hill, pulling the eye and the player along one route
dirt, tall grass and bright blue water read as three distinct surfaces, so walkable ground is obvious without markers
torches on short pillars make evenly spaced warm pools along a stone hall, so the player can count the distance to the next doorway
warm brown stone, orange timber and a cool purple-lit floor split the frame into walls, ceiling and walkable ground by colour temperature
a walled village in a bowl of tall cliffs reads as one destination, with the gatehouse wall as the approach landmark
warm sandstone walls, saturated grass and cool grey-blue cliffs separate built space, open ground and boundary at a glance

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Under D-UIONLY-1 every element comes from insert_ui_component with genre 'adventure'; these rules say which components, where, and how they relate. They set no px values, because none were measured.

vitalsStack.rule: Health, mana and experience are ONE stacked assembly in one corner: a thin experience bar on top, the thickest health bar in the middle, a thin mana bar below. Build it from health_bar, progress_bar and level_bar placed as a column.
vitalsStack.never: three separate bars scattered to different screen edges
vitalsStack.why: the one adventure HUD study in the set stacks all three in a shared frame and makes health the focal element, so a player reads their state in one glance at one place

resourceColours.why: the resource-bar study fixes one colour family per resource and proves the choice with a swatch study before the art, which is what lets a player read a bar by colour alone

numberInsideFill.rule: The health readout is a number right-aligned inside the health fill, set through the component's text/value, not a separate label beside the bar.
numberInsideFill.why: the reference sets the number inside the fill so the value and the bar are read together without the eye leaving the bar

enemyNameplate.rule: Enemies carry a billboard_tag above the head: name on the left, level on the right, health bar beneath both.
enemyNameplate.why: the classic-RPG reference shows exactly this layout on every enemy, so the player learns threat level before engaging without opening any menu

damageNumbers.rule: Damage is a separate floating number above the target, apart from the nameplate, in the health colour.
damageNumbers.never: damage shown only as the nameplate bar shrinking
damageNumbers.why: the reference shows hits as large red floating numbers separate from the nameplate, so a hit is read without looking at a bar

chestInventory.rule: A chest or bag is an inventory_grid of equal square slots with a full-width search field above it and a footer that reads the container name and used/maximum slots.
chestInventory.why: the inventory reference filters a large chest by search instead of scrolling, and its capacity footer keeps the storage limit visible while sorting

emptySlotContrast.rule: Empty slots must contrast visibly with the panel behind them; a themed wood panel does not excuse the grid disappearing.
emptySlotContrast.why: the inventory reference shows the failure directly: its empty slots sit so close to the brown panel that the grid edges nearly vanish

merchantAtTheCounter.rule: A merchant shop sells from the world: items on shelves, each with a surface_sign carrying its name, price and buy button, opened by one interact prompt at the counter.
merchantAtTheCounter.never: a full-screen shop catalogue as the only way to buy from an in-world merchant
merchantAtTheCounter.why: the shop reference keeps browsing at the counter where the player already stands, so the purchase feels like visiting a place rather than opening a menu

worldCarriesTheRoute.rule: Wayfinding is built into the world: signposts and notice boards where the route turns, and lantern or torch chains at night or underground. Do not add a HUD arrow unless the build asks for one.
worldCarriesTheRoute.why: four of the eight references (village path, open-world night road, dungeon hall, castle valley) guide the player with signposts, light chains and landmarks, and none of them shows an on-screen arrow

hudLeavesTheSceneOpen.rule: Keep the always-on HUD to the vitals stack and nameplates. Inventory, shop and settings open as windows on demand.
hudLeavesTheSceneOpen.why: every adventure reference that sells the genre does it with the scene (landmarks, lit routes, readable materials), so a HUD that covers the view removes the thing players came for

ratchetNote: Eight references, above the five-reference minimum in tests/ui-references.test.mjs. The weakest point is the always-on HUD: one study of the vitals stack and one of the nameplates. Add a shipped adventure game's HUD before tightening any geometry here.
